sources.cite: Zhu, Yang & Hsee (2018), "The Mere Urgency Effect," J. Consumer Research 45(3):673-690
sources.design: 5 experiments; Exp.1 lab (N=124, Hershey's Kisses payoffs); Exp.2A/2B MTurk (N=203/204, cents payoffs, attentional-focus mediation); Exp.3 MTurk (outcome-salience moderator, not read this session); Exp.4 MTurk (perceived-busyness moderator, not read this session)
sources.n: Exp.1 N=124; Exp.2A N=203; Exp.2B N=204
sources.effect: Categorical dominance violation, replicated across Exp.1/2A/2B with chi-square tests; mediated by attentional focus (more thoughts of expiration time, fewer of payoffs, under urgency)
sources.finding_quote: Gap-fill (2026-09-25): downloaded the primary PDF directly and read Experiments 1, 2A and 2B in full this session (Experiment 3's outcome-salience test was not reached -- see unverified below). Abstract (verbatim, as before): 'The current research identifies a mere urgency effect...' Experiment 1 (verbatim): '13.3% of students chose to work on the low-payoff task in the control condition, whereas 31.3% of students chose to work on it in the urgency condition, chi-square(1)=5.69, p=.017, phi=.21.' Experiment 2A (verbatim): '13.9% of workers chose to work on the low-payoff task in the control condition, whereas 35.3% of workers chose to work on the low-payoff task in the urgency condition, chi-square(1)=11.43, p<.001, phi=.24.' Mediation (verbatim): urgency-condition participants were more likely to mention expiration time (41.2% vs 1.0%, p<.001) and less likely to mention payoffs (69.6% vs 82.2%, p=.036) than control; relative attentional focus mediated the urgency-to-choice effect (beta=1.42, SE=.46, 95% CI [.87, 2.21]).

sources.cite: Mills, Cubitt & Starmer (2026), "Brief Commentary: An Independent Replication Study of the Mere Urgency Effect," J. Consumer Research
sources.design: Independent large-scale replication: base design following Zhu et al. 2018, plus confound-controlled variants, plus a new 'fresh eyes' design, plus meta-analytic synthesis across replications
sources.effect: MUE attenuated once confounds are controlled, but remains significant in every variant tested
sources.finding_quote: An extensive, independent replication study (n = 2,374) of the Mere Urgency Effect (MUE) (Zhu et al. 2018) is reported... Although the MUE is attenuated by adding controls to the base design, a significant MUE is found in all tests designed to control for confounds, including the new setup. Hence, the existence of an MUE that is robust to variations in experimental design and to controls for the mechanisms conjectured as potential confounds is confirmed.

backfire.condition: Effect size shrinks once experimenter-demand and other confounds are controlled for in the base design, though it does not vanish.

sources.design: Multiple purchase-decision experiments with cues prompting consideration of opportunity costs
